title: Use easier motion-mapped variants before extreme one-to-one mimic tasks
summary: If the player's response pattern is weak, easier scenarios that teach the core movement cleanly will usually transfer better than jumping straight into the most game-like or most reactive variant.
why: Direct stimulus mapping fails if the player still performs the wrong response to that stimulus.
Easier motion-mapped variants let the player build the right movement before the fully punishing version exposes every flaw.
actions: If your game-specific task is very reactive, first find the easier scenario that trains the same movement relationship more cleanly.
Build the correction pattern and micro-adjustment angle first, then add harsher reactive variants later.
Use the harder one-to-one scenario as a later transfer check instead of as your starting point.
avoid: Do not start with the harshest direct-game mimic scenario if the base movement is still wrong.

drills.label: Reactive control before reactive speed
drills.query: manageable reactive tracking control before speed
drills.reason: A manageable reactive variant helps establish the correct response pattern before pure difficulty takes over.

evidence.claim: Beginners should often start with easier variants that train the movement basics instead of the most direct one-to-one game-like reactive task.
evidence.excerpt: You shouldn't be starting off with scenarios that provide a direct stimulus mapping, but easier variants that train the basics of the movements themselves.
